title: PEOPLE
blurb: Who we are, what we say and how we feel.

radicals.name: PERSON
radicals.origin: 人 is a person walking, seen from the side. Squeezed onto the left of a character, the two legs fold up into 亻.
ex: a person: the one in front of me
a person leaning on a tree 木
radicals.watch: Hundreds of characters carry 亻, so the hint is broad. In 件 (jiàn, an item) or 化 (huà, to change) the person is hard to find.

radicals.name: WOMAN
radicals.origin: The oldest form shows a kneeling figure with crossed arms. As a radical it keeps its shape and gets a little narrower.
ex: a woman, plus 马 for the sound
他 with the person swapped for a woman
a woman with a child 子
radicals.watch: 女 can also sit at the bottom, as in 要 (yào, to want). Some old characters with 女 are unkind to women; they tell you about ancient attitudes, not about the language today.

radicals.name: MOUTH
radicals.origin: An open mouth, drawn as a box. It is one of the few radicals that still looks like its picture.
radicals.watch: 口 also marks little spoken words with no meaning of their own, such as 吗, 吧 and 呢. The big box that wraps a whole character, as in 国 (country), is a different radical: 囗, an enclosure.

radicals.name: SPEECH
radicals.origin: 言 shows words rising out of a mouth 口. Simplified Chinese shrinks it to two quick strokes when it stands on the left.
radicals.watch: 讠 exists only on the left. Anywhere else the full form stays, as in 信 (xìn, a letter): a person 亻 standing by their word 言.

radicals.name: HEART
radicals.origin: 心 is a drawing of the heart. On the left it stands up straight as 忄. At the bottom it keeps its full shape.
ex: the full 心 sits at the bottom
radicals.watch: In Chinese the heart thinks as well as feels, so 心 covers the mind too: 想 (think), 忘 (forget), 意 (idea).
